title: Relationships between dog caregiving, stress coping, and online peer support: A mixed-methods study of parent and adolescent perspectives
abstract: Abstract Background: Adolescence is a critical developmental period of seeking social connection as well as coping with stress related to those relationships. Little is known about whether the peer relationships that become so crucial during adolescence might be associated with an adolescent’s ability and motivation to take care of their pets. In addition, few studies examine pet caregiving from both the parents’ and adolescents’ perspectives. Methods: This mixed-methods study of US parents and adolescents (aged 13–17) employed survey and interview methods to analyze relationships between dog caregiving, coping with peer stress, and seeking online peer support. Results: We found that adaptive coping with peer stress was significantly associated with dog caregiving, whereas maladaptive coping was not associated with dog caregiving. A unique finding of social media help-seeking was significantly associated with stress coping strategies and involvement with dog caregiving in the home. Parent interviews emphasized observable behaviors such as self-isolation in bedrooms or scrolling on phones as maladaptive coping strategies; however, adolescent interviews also revealed the content of their online activities that included social support-seeking, sharing dog stories and photos/videos, and seeking positive content to regulate their emotions. Conclusions: These findings have implications for parents, counselors, and social workers who want guidance in affirming that peer stress does not seem to deter adolescents from taking care of their pet dogs; in fact, the more they nurture their pets, the better they cope with peer stress as well as seek online social support.
